# The Lantern Road

Mara saw the lamp flicker and felt the cold creep in. She noticed the door stood open.

"Get out," Aldric hissed.

"Not yet," Mara said quietly.

Mara was furious at the delay.

"One," Aldric whispered.

"Two," Mara whispered.

"Three," Bellmere whispered.

He walked to the door. He opened it. He looked outside.

The silver lantern swung above the silver gate.

The river carried leaves past the quiet mill. A heron stood motionless near the far bank. Smoke drifted from the chimney of the cottage. Children were calling somewhere beyond the orchard wall. The baker opened his shutters to the morning. Nobody on the lane spoke of the storm.

The market spread across the square in a crowd of canvas awnings and hand-painted signs, and every stall carried something different: copper kettles, bundled herbs, bolts of dyed wool, jars of pickled eggs, carved wooden toys, and tins of tea from the far south, while the vendors called out prices to anyone who slowed, and ragged musicians and stray dogs wandered through the shifting crowd until the bells rang noon.

She counted the broken stairs one by one.

Dusk settled over the harbor town as lamplighters made their rounds along the narrow lanes, trading gossip with shopkeepers who were pulling in their awnings for the night.

Later she counted the broken stairs again.

Aldric led the way past the old customs house. Bellmere did not look back. Aldrick's cart stood waiting at the corner.

# The Tide Tables

Gulls wheeled over the jetty. The harbormaster sighed heavily and slowly unrolled the chart, then carefully pinned each corner against the gusting wind. Fishermen nodded politely, grumbled quietly, and eventually shuffled aside. Nobody spoke of the missing skiff, though suddenly everyone seemed to remember an errand elsewhere. The tide would turn within the hour.

# The Glass Room

Beyond the doorway the hall opened into a gleaming chamber, bright with crimson banners and golden trim. Shadows pooled beneath each arch while pale lanterns cast a glitter across the polished floor, and a single silhouette crossed the far wall. Nothing about the room suggested that anyone had entered it for years.

# The Quiet Count

The ferry left at dawn. It returned by dusk with a different crew every time it crossed the wide water of the bay.

Orchard keepers gathered apples before the first frost. They stacked every crate inside the barn, safe from rain and hungry mice all winter.

Nobody remembered when the old bridge collapsed. Villagers simply learned to cross the river without it, and the habit outlived the memory.

Schoolchildren recited the names of streams that wound across the continent toward coasts. Their teachers pointed at faded maps pinned beside the window.

Merchants argued over the price of salt, since every season brought some fresh complaint from the inland towns and a new tax.

Travelers who stayed through the winter found that the village kept its own calendar. Markets and feasts marked the turning of each year.
